A close reading for the week

“Blow, winds, and crack your cheeks!”

King Lear · Act 3, Scene 2

Shut out of both his daughters’ houses, Lear stands in open country and gives orders to the weather. The commands cannot be obeyed, and in the middle of them, for the first time, the king begins to describe himself accurately.

LEARBlow, winds, and crack your cheeks! Rage! blow!1
You cataracts and hurricanoes, spout
Till you have drench’d our steeples, drown’d the cocks!2
You sulphurous and thought-executing fires,
Vaunt-couriers to oak-cleaving thunderbolts,
Singe my white head! And thou, all-shaking thunder,
Strike flat the thick rotundity o’ the world!
Crack nature’s moulds, all germens spill at once,
That make ingrateful man!

  1. 1

    Orders no one can obey

    Old maps drew the winds as faces with puffed cheeks, blowing across the sea; Lear commands those faces to blow until they burst. The speech is built of imperatives (blow, rage, spout, singe, strike, crack), the grammar of a king. But weather takes no orders, so royal command survives here only as a form, with nothing left that must obey it.

  2. 2

    A second Flood

    “Cataracts” are the floodgates of heaven; “hurricanoes” were waterspouts, a new and exotic word in English. Drowned steeples and weathercocks put whole towns underwater. Lear wants more than shelter, or revenge on two women: he is asking for something on the scale of Noah’s deluge.
